To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the chemotherapeutic sensitivity of ALL cell lines in culture correlates well with that in donor patients.

the sensitivity of four ALL lines to chemotherapeutic drugs was measured by clonogenic assay; two different criteria of sensitivity based on concentrations derived from pharmacokinetics in man were used; and although a good correlation between in vitro and in vivo responses to chemotherapeutic treatment of the donor patients was obtained for some drugs, no new cut-off line was found to satisfy completely in vivo/in vitro correlation for all the agents.
the sensitivity of ALL cell lines to chemotherapeutic drugs can be predicted from in vivo pharmacokinetics and that the correlation is not perfect.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a predictive test for chemotherapeutic sensitivity in acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL) patients.
the establishment of permanent acute leukemic cell lines of different phenotypic types and their sensitivity to various chemotherapeutic agents by means of clonal assays.
the study of acute lymphocytic leukemic cells in culture, and the establishment of permanent lines from patients has permitted us to study their chemotherapeutic sensitivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the in vitro system, although not yet fully developed, can provide useful information in the evaluation of new chemotherapeutic agents.
in vitro sensitivity testing of ALL lines is not predictive of the clinical course in the donor patients.
the correlation of the in vitro data to in vivo data is not yet satisfactory, although the data are encouraging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single criterion for in vitro sensitivity testing may not suffice to predict the clinical course of ALL patients.
the in vitro system can be used to study the sensitivity of acute leukemia cells to chemotherapeutic drugs and that the results obtained can be used to predict the response of the donor patients.
the in vitro system, although useful for the study of chemotherapeutic mechanisms, has not yet reached its full potential in predictive testing of chemotherapeutic agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single criterion for the in vitro sensitivity of ALL cells may not be appropriate.

the clonogenic assay is a valuable tool to study the chemotherapeutic response of acute lymphocytic leukemias and that a combination of both pharmacokinetic parameters and the clonogenic response may provide a more reliable system for predictive testing of new agents in the treatment of acute lymphocitic leukemia.
in vitro testing may not always correlate with in vivo clinical response.
